sessions.narration:
The Trade Way ends here, in a jam of wheels, hooves and tempers beneath the grey arch of the Basilisk Gate. The sun is low over the Sword Coast and the first lanterns are flickering along the wall. Somewhere beyond the stone is Baldur's Gate — the city from the stories, where a goddess told you that you would learn how to serve her. She did not say how.

At the table under the arch a Flaming Fist sergeant with a scarred chin and an ink-stained ledger waves the next traveller forward, asks a question, and writes without looking up. A halfling in a patched green coat slips along the queue, calling out: "Clean beds, Outer City prices, no fleas worth mentioning!"

Behind you, a slap of cards on wood and a burst of laughter: the caravan guards have started another hand on an upturned barrel. A gust of wind lifts a card off their makeshift table, and it skids to a stop against your boot, face-down. The cat looks at it, then at you.

The man in front of you is waved through. The sergeant dips her quill and looks up. "Next. Name, and what brings you to the Gate?"

sessions.narration:
The gangplank thumps against the stones of the Gull Steps, and Baldur's Gate rises before you in the last light: warehouses shouldered together, smoke from a hundred chimneys, the dark line of the wall above the roofs and, higher still, the lamps of the Upper City. The quay smells of tar, fish and river mud. Copper the cat flows down the plank ahead of you and sits on a bollard as though he has lived here all his life.

At the head of the steps a Flaming Fist sergeant with an ink-stained thumb sits behind a trestle table, a ledger open in front of him. "Name, business, how long you're staying," he calls to each passenger in turn, without looking up much. A wiry porter is already sizing up your pack. "Carry it to a decent inn for two silvers, ser? Or a cheap one for one, and I won't say which is which."

A little way off, between two stacks of crates, a lantern hangs over an upturned barrel. A tiefling dealer with silver rings on every finger flicks cards to three dockhands. The fourth place is an empty stool — and in front of it lies a hand, already dealt, face-down. Nobody reaches for it. The dealer glances your way, just once, and goes back to the game.

The sergeant's quill scratches. "Next." The line moves, and you are next.

sessions.narration:
The gangplank of the Saltwind bumps against the stones, and Baldur's Gate rises in front of you: tarred hulls, wet rope, smoke from a hundred chimneys, and the long climb of roofs toward the wall where the patriars live. The sun is going down behind the masts; the lamplighters are already at work.

The queue from the ship shuffles toward a trestle table under a Flaming Fist banner. Behind it a sergeant with ink on her fingers and a long day in her face looks up at each newcomer: "Name. Business in the Gate. Next."

Off to the side, on an upturned crate, three cards flick and slide under a young man's quick hands. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady — Tymora smiles on the bold!" A dockhand groans and loses a copper. The dealer's eyes travel along the queue and settle on you.

At your feet the cat has gone very still, ears forward, staring at the doorway of a warehouse across the quay. The doorway is dark and, as far as you can see, empty.

The sergeant's quill is waiting. "You. Name, and what brings you to the city?"

sessions.narration:
The gangplank bows under your boots, and then there is stone: Lantern Quay, slick with the day's spray and loud with Baldur's Gate. Gulls quarrel over the fish stalls. Porters shout each other out of the way. Above the warehouse roofs the city climbs towards the inner wall, where the first lamps of the Upper City are being lit against a copper sky. Penny pads down the plank beside you, tail high, and stops at the last board. A single copper coin lies there face-up, clean, as if someone had just set it down. The crowd steps around it without a glance.

Ahead, a Flaming Fist sergeant with an ink-stained ledger is working through the arrivals one name at a time. "Name. Business in the Gate. Next." A barefoot girl darts along the line, tugging sleeves: "Bed for the night? Clean straw, no fleas, I'll take you there for a copper!" From beyond the crates comes the soft snap of a shuffled deck and a woman's voice, warm and practised: "Find the lady, friends — one silver to play, three if your eye's sharper than my hand."

The line shuffles forward. The sergeant's pen is already lifting towards you. The coin still lies at your feet, and the cat is looking at it — then up at you.

sessions.narration:
The bridge never quite stops moving. Carts creak over the stones, a fishwife bawls prices from a window overhead, and the Chionthar slaps at the piers below. After weeks on the road, Baldur's Gate is right in front of you: one wall, one narrow gate, and a line of tired people who all want to get through before full dark.

At the gate sits Sergeant Odessa Varn of the Flaming Fist, red cloak stained, ledger open. Her face says she has asked the same two questions a thousand times today. Up ahead, a tiefling father with two children has been waved out of the line to stand by the barrels, and he is holding his papers very tightly.

Off to your left a voice cuts through the noise, warm as mulled wine: "Three cards, friends, one queen! Find the lady, double your silver! The Lady's watching tonight, I can feel it!" Ferro Lask flicks the cards across his crate with a dealer's easy hands, and the sound of them is one you know very well.

The cat sits down on the cobbles, tail curled, and stares up at the gatepost. Someone has chalked a small coin there, a circle with a face in it, so fresh the dust hasn't settled.

The line shuffles forward. Varn glances up from her ledger, past the man in front of you, and finds you.

"Next. Name, and what's your business in the Gate?"

sessions.narration: Dusk settles over the Chionthar as you step onto Wyrm's Crossing. The bridge is less a bridge than a street hung over the water: shopfronts jammed shoulder to shoulder, washing strung between upper windows, hawkers selling hot eels and fried dough to anyone who slows down. Ahead, the Basilisk Gate rises dark against the last of the light, and before it a queue grinds forward past a Flaming Fist checkpoint. A broad-shouldered sergeant in a red-trimmed tabard is reading papers by lantern light, pulling a cart aside here, waving a family through there, and casting a long look at a pair of tiefling porters. Your cat walks close to your boots, tail high, ears turning at every shout. Then, off to one side, a voice cuts through the noise: "Three cards, friends, one queen — find the Lady and she pays double!" Under a lamp, a lean man in a patched green coat shuffles a deck on an upturned barrel, fingers quick and easy. Two dockhands are already playing. And at the empty side of the barrel, where a third player would sit, lies a single coin with Tymora's smiling face turned up — placed with care, untouched, as if the seat were reserved. The dealer catches your eye, and his smile widens. "You've the look of a man the Lady likes. Sit a hand?" Behind you, the queue to the gate shuffles forward a step. The lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge, and the city is waiting on the other side of the wall.

sessions.narration:
The sun drops behind the masts downriver, and Wyrm's Crossing fills with lantern light and the smell of frying fish. The bridge is less a road than a street built on stone. Shutters bang, a fishwife haggles over the last eels, and a porter swears at a mule that will not move. At the far end a barrier of rough planks blocks the way, painted with the Flaming Fist's red gauntlet. Behind it a broad-shouldered sergeant with ink on her fingers works through the queue. She asks each traveller the same question, takes their coppers, scratches a line in a ledger and waves them on.

The cat walks the parapet beside you as if it owns the bridge. At the barrier post it stops and sniffs a chalk mark on the stone. The mark is fresh, not yet smudged by rain or boots, and it is Tymora's coin-sign, face up. Nobody in the queue looks at it.

Just past the barrier, under a hanging lantern, a gnome in a patched velvet coat shuffles a deck with practised fingers on an upturned crate. "One hand, friends, just one, Lady Luck's awake tonight!" The cards whisper as they fall.

The merchant ahead of you pays and steps through. The sergeant dips her pen, looks up and fixes you with a tired, measuring stare. "Next. Name, and what's your business in the Gate?"

sessions.narration:
Dusk settles over Baldur's Gate like soot. Behind you the Outer City is still shouting: a carter curses a stuck wheel, a woman sells skewered eel from a smoking brazier, and two tiefling children dodge a Flaming Fist patrol that pretends not to see them. Ahead, the gate's arch swallows the line one traveller at a time. Beyond it the Lower City slopes down toward the harbour, and the first tavern lamps are coming on along the street.

The cat walks at your heel, tail high, as if the city belongs to it. Halfway through the arch it stops and stares. Just inside the gate, a lean man in a frayed green coat has set an upturned barrel under a lantern. He fans a deck across the lid with an easy flick that has nothing to do with chance. "One hand, friends, one hand before supper. Lady Luck's awake at this hour," he calls. Nobody has sat down yet.

A halfling no taller than your belt falls into step beside you. "New in the Gate? Bed, bath, beer, and nobody robs you before breakfast. A copper and I'll take you there."

Then the line moves, and you reach the trestle table. The Flaming Fist sergeant behind it has a burn scar along her jaw and ink on her fingers. She glances at your cloak, at the crossbow, at the cat, and finally at your face.

"Name," she says, dipping her pen. "Business in the city. And the toll. Next."

sessions.narration:
Grey light slips through the shutters. Down the street a forge hammer strikes, then another, until Beregost has its morning rhythm. Bells sound from the temple of Lathander. The cat is already up, sitting on the windowsill with its tail curled, watching the street as if it owns it. The purse on the chair is heavy: about three hundred and fifty gold, all that is left of the last hand.

Someone knocks three times, brisk and practised. "Morning, master Worgen," calls Marta Holloway, the innkeeper, through the door. "Breakfast's on below, porridge and bacon. Will you be keeping the room another night? Two silver, same as before." She pauses. "And a fellow at the bar was asking whether a man with a cat was stopping here. Didn't give a name. I didn't give him yours."

sessions.narration:
Beregost wakes the way a smiths' town does. First one hammer rings, then a dozen, and a temple bell answers them from somewhere over the rooftops. Pale light comes through the shutters and lies across the floorboards and the heavy purse on the stool. Last night's luck still weighs about three hundred and fifty gold.

There are no orders, no caravan to guard and no debt to collect today. From below come the clatter of plates, the smell of bacon and new bread, and the innkeeper's voice calling someone a fool.

The cat sits on the windowsill with its tail curled around its paws. It is not looking at the street. It is looking at the door. A moment ago the stairs creaked, and footsteps came up and stopped just outside. Nobody knocked. After a few breaths the steps went back down, unhurried.

sessions.narration:
Morning finds you before you find it: a thin bar of light through the shutters, the clang of the first forge hammer somewhere down the street, and the slow bronze voice of Lathander's bells rolling over the rooftops of Beregost. The room above the Lantern and Anvil smells of old timber, cold ashes and fresh bread drifting up the stairs.

Your cat sits on the windowsill, tail curled neatly around its paws, watching you with the patience of a creature that has been awake for hours. Beside it, face up on the sill, lies a playing card: the queen of coins, its edges soft with handling. Your own deck is where you left it. This card is not from it, and it was not there last night.

From the yard below comes the rattle of dice in a cup, a burst of laughter and someone cursing their luck. A knock sounds at the door, and a young woman's voice calls through it: "Master Worgen? Hot water, if you want it, and there's porridge and sausages downstairs while they last."

The purse is heavy, the day is empty, and the queen of coins looks up at you from the windowsill. What do you do?

sessions.narration:
Dawn finds its way through the gaps in the shutters and lays thin gold lines across the floorboards. Somewhere down the street a hammer strikes iron, then another joins it. Beregost's forges are waking. Over the rooftops, the bells of the Morninglord's temple roll out their slow greeting to the sun.

The cat is already up. It sits on the windowsill with its tail curled around its paws, watching the street below with keen interest. Now and then it turns to look at you, as if wondering why you are still in bed.

Your purse lies where you left it, heavy with about three hundred and fifty gold from that last hand. The road to Baldur's Gate runs north past the window. Nobody expects you anywhere today.

From below come the smell of frying bacon and the scrape of benches. Under that is a sound you would know anywhere: cards being shuffled and slapped down on wood, and a rough laugh. "Raise you two silver, and may Tymora weep for you!"

Then three brisk knocks at your door. "Master Worgen?" It is a woman's voice, the innkeeper's. "Breakfast's on, if you want it. And I need to know whether you're keeping the room another night, or whether I let it to the caravan folk who came in late."

The cat's ears twitch toward the door. The latch waits.
